technical_body.purpose: Indicate trunk idle/busy state on a 4-wire analog interoffice trunk (Bell system).

semantics.seizure: far-end CO drops tone -> seizure detected
semantics.disconnect: near-end reapplies tone after answer -> disconnect signaled

technical_body.attack_surface: The blue-box seizure attack. Play 2600 Hz into the audio path after answer supervision for ~400-1000 ms depending on the far-end switch; the originating tandem interprets this as far-end on-hook, drops the trunk to a wink/idle while the near-end loop stays up, letting the phreak MF-pulse a fresh destination.
technical_body.died_because: Migration to CCIS (No.6) and then SS7 moved trunk supervision out-of-band. AT&T Long Lines completed CCIS on major routes by early 1980s; SF/MF ran on independents into the mid-1990s.
technical_body.detection: 1AESS generic 1AE7+ and 4ESS added '2600 Hz hold time exceeded' alarms. AT&T greenstar/blueflag programs logged suspicious patterns from the 1970s.

technical_body.purpose: Address (inter-register) signaling on 4-wire analog interoffice trunks — the digits that follow SF seizure.
technical_body.encoding: two-of-six frequency pairs; six tones total
technical_body.digits_expressed: 0-9, KP (start of address), ST (end of address), plus control codes at 700+1700 / 900+1700 / 1300+1700
technical_body.international_address_format: KP + 011 + CC + national_number + ST (on international-capable trunks)
technical_body.died_because: Same reason as SF — CCIS/SS7 moved signaling out-of-band.
distinguish_from: DTMF (Q.23) — subscriber-loop only, different frequency set (697-1633 Hz)
MF R2 / MFC (Q.441) — used in LATAM/Europe/Asia, different frequencies (1140-1980 Hz)
CCITT No.5 inter-register — reuses the same R1 frequencies, but different line-signaling tones (2400+2600)

technical_body.purpose: International in-band trunk signaling on TAT and similar cables between national gateways.

line_signaling.answer_clear_back_clear_forward: encoded as pulse patterns of 2400 and 2600 used singly and combined

technical_body.inter_register_signaling: Same MF frequency set as R1 (700-1700 Hz); same KP + digits + ST format.
technical_body.attack_surface: The 'international blue box' story ('Chevy Chase, Maryland' TAT-6/TAT-7 ops late 70s/early 80s). Crucially: a device that emits ONLY 2600 Hz will NOT seize a No.5 trunk — the seizure signal is 2400 Hz. This is a common DEFCON trap.
technical_body.died_because: No.5 trunks converted to No.6 (CCIS) and No.7 (SS7) in the 1980s. Persisted on some third-world routes into the mid-1990s (community reports; primary confirmation weak).

disputed.persistence: Community memory reports vulnerable No.5 gateways on Caribbean and West African routes into the mid-1990s; ITU switching-plan reports do not confirm this cleanly. Mark community-provenance.

technical_body.purpose: In-band trunk signaling widely deployed in LATAM, Iberia, parts of Asia and Africa. NOT compatible with R1.
technical_body.line_signaling_analog: Compelled tones at 3825 Hz (forward and backward). NOT 2600 Hz — a common confusion.

inter_register_signaling_mfc.encoding: compelled MF: forward tone stays on until backward tone acknowledges, then both cease
inter_register_signaling_mfc.group_context: Meaning of each combination is context-dependent — Group I / II forward, Group A / B backward. Any R2 record must specify the group.
inter_register_signaling_mfc.notes: Backward tones are LOWER than forward tones (opposite convention from R1).

technical_body.died_because: Digital signaling (SS7/C7) rollouts in each country. Persisted longer in LATAM than R1 did in NANP — into the late 1990s in some operators.

technical_body.purpose: First out-of-band inter-office signaling system — separate data channel between switches for call setup, teardown, and management.
technical_body.carrier: dedicated 2.4-4.8 kbps data channel between offices, later 56/64 kbps
technical_body.topology: point-to-point predecessor to the fully-associated STP mesh of SS7
technical_body.impact: The change that killed classical blue boxing. Once signaling moved off the voice band, a 2600 Hz tone injected into the audio path became just audio — the far end no longer read it as supervision.
technical_body.rollout: AT&T Long Lines began CCIS deployment 1976; major routes completed by early 1980s. Transitioned to No.7 in the mid-1980s.
technical_body.died_because: Superseded by SS7 (No.7) starting 1980; last CCIS links replaced by mid-1980s in AT&T. Independents lagged.

technical_body.purpose: Universal out-of-band signaling protocol. Runs between STPs (Signaling Transfer Points) on 56/64 kbps links (classical) or SIGTRAN (M3UA/SUA over SCTP over IP) in modern deployments.
technical_body.rollout: Introduced 1980 (CCIS/No.6 -> No.7); ANSI SS7 standardized 1988; ubiquitous on North American interoffice trunks by ~1992.
technical_body.phreak_relevance_era: Out-of-scope for classic-phreak (in-band) attacks — SS7 introduces its own attack class (SCCP/TCAP/MAP abuse, Global Title spoofing, MAP-AnyTimeInterrogation, SMS home-routing bypass) that became public research 2008+ (Tobias Engel, Karsten Nohl, Sergey Puzankov). Modern SS7 attacks are a separate, post-era volume.

technical_body.purpose: Subscriber-to-CO address signaling — the tones a phone sends when you press keys.
technical_body.encoding: one low + one high frequency per key
technical_body.keys: 0-9, *, #, plus A/B/C/D on the 1633 Hz column (military/AUTOVON)
distinguish_from: MF R1 — inter-office, six-tone set (700-1700), CO-to-CO only
AUTOVON — same DTMF frequencies plus the 1633 Hz column keys for precedence

name: AUTOVON — the Autovon military dial plan

technical_body.purpose: DoD Automatic Voice Network — DTMF-plus-precedence military dial plan on dedicated switches (Class-A) with off-net access to civilian PSTN.
technical_body.preemption_semantics: Pressing a precedence key before dialing causes the switch to preempt any lower-precedence traffic on shared trunks.
technical_body.successor: DSN (Defense Switched Network) inherited the precedence concept but replaced the DTMF-key mechanism with ISDN precedence and, later, IP-based Assured Services (AS-SIP RPH, ETS).
technical_body.died_because: AUTOVON decommissioned ~1990 in favor of DSN.

disputed.cd_reversal: Community sources sometimes reverse C and D (calling D=Immediate and C=Priority). MIL-STD-187-100 is authoritative: A=FO, B=F, C=I, D=P.

technical_body.purpose: The default subscriber-loop supervision on POTS. The subscriber's phone signals off-hook by closing a DC loop across the tip-and-ring pair to the CO's battery feed.
technical_body.signaling: tip-and-ring DC loop closure = off-hook. CO applies 48V battery with ~-48V on ring and ground on tip when idle; loop current flows when the subscriber lifts the handset.
technical_body.ring: CO superimposes ~90V RMS 20 Hz AC ring voltage on the loop
distinguish_from: ground-start (uses ground signal on the ring lead)
reverse-battery (CO reverses tip/ring polarity for answer supervision)
quirks: Glare — race condition where both ends seize simultaneously; more common on loop-start PBX trunks than ground-start
No CO -> subscriber disconnect signal — the subscriber can hold the loop indefinitely after the far end hangs up

technical_body.purpose: Alternative to loop-start on PBX trunks. Reduces glare — one end grounds the tip lead to seize, the other end recognizes and grounds ring in response.
technical_body.signaling: PBX side grounds tip; CO recognizes and grounds ring after ~100 ms. Both ends then know a call is in progress before ring voltage is applied.
technical_body.typical_use: PBX-to-CO trunks, especially DID trunks. Rarely on single-line residential POTS.

technical_body.purpose: Signal from the terminating CO back to the originating CO that the far party has answered — reverses the polarity of battery on the tip/ring pair.
technical_body.attack_surface: The black-box attack. A resistor/capacitor circuit across the called party's loop prevents polarity reversal from being detected, so the originating CO believes the call was never answered and does not bill.
technical_body.died_because: Answer supervision moved out-of-band once CCIS/SS7 delivered it as an ISUP ANM message; keeping the local loop off-hook no longer masks answer.

technical_body.purpose: DC-signaled trunk interfaces between switches or between a switch and a channel bank. E-lead ('Ear', receive) and M-lead ('Mouth', transmit) carry the supervision state.

types.Type I: M-lead source of battery, E-lead source of ground. Common in North America.
types.Type II: Symmetric; both leads referenced through a common signal battery/ground
types.Type III: M-lead: battery+ground; E-lead: ground when on-hook, open when off-hook. Rare.
types.Type IV: Fully symmetric double-battery arrangement — used for long haul with intermediate repeaters
types.Type V: Common in Europe; both leads switched-ground

technical_body.usage: Interconnects between colocated switches / PBX to channel bank. Rarely seen by end users but critical for how a PBX exchanges answer supervision with an old CO trunk.

technical_body.purpose: In-band supervision on a digital T-1 trunk. Steals the least-significant bit of every 6th frame of each channel for signaling bits (A/B/C/D in Extended Superframe format).
technical_body.carrier: 1.544 Mbps DS1 — 24 DS0 x 64 kbps + 8 kbps framing
technical_body.signaling_state_encoding: A/B/C/D bits map to loop-start / ground-start / E&M supervision states depending on trunk type
technical_body.impact: Because the LSB is stolen, each DS0 delivers 56 kbps clear data instead of 64 kbps — the reason dial-up modems topped out at 56 k on TDM channels.
technical_body.distinguish_from: ISDN PRI (23B+D or 30B+D) — signaling on the D channel means full 64 kbps per B channel with no robbed bits

technical_body.purpose: In-band delivery of Automatic Number Identification (ANI) and info-digit prefix on Feature Group D trunks — the mechanism that lets a downstream IXC or 8YY termination know who called.
technical_body.sequence: originating CO seizes trunk -> far end returns a 150-200 ms 'wink' (off-hook, on-hook) as go-ahead -> originating CO spills 'KP + II + KP + ANI + ST' in MF, where II is the 2-digit info-digit prefix (see ani_ii_00 through ani_ii_reserved_range) and ANI is 10 digits.
technical_body.successor: SS7 ISUP OLI parameter (hex 00-63) + CgPN (calling party number)
technical_body.phreak_relevance: Injecting your own II bits at the right moment lets you impersonate a class (fake AIOD, hide payphone origin). Early PC-based tools like 'ANI II Sniffer' sat on 8YY terminations logging the info-digit byte for every inbound call.

technical_body.purpose: Concentrates up to 96 (later 2000+) subscriber lines onto a small number of digital trunks back to the CO — the green cabinet on the sidewalk.
technical_body.impact_on_signaling: Once a subscriber is served by an SLC, their loop no longer directly reaches the CO switch's line card. Loop signaling terminates at the SLC's remote terminal (RT), which then hauls audio + signaling back to the central office terminal (COT) over T1 or GR-303 fiber. Some in-band tricks (e.g. blue-box seizure against a distant far-end CO) still work; others (like reading local loop-current signaling directly) don't — you're now talking to a concentrator, not the switch.
technical_body.prevalence: By 1995, ~40% of US access lines were behind some form of SLC. By 2010, ~70%.
